newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition says main battles still to come.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition says main battles still to come.

text.p: BELGRADE, Feb 10, Reuter - Serbia's political opposition, on the eve of a triumph over President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling socialists, said the main battles for democratic reform were still to come.
"There will be protests throughout the year. History has shown that Milosevic has conceded nothing without street demonstrations," Democratic Party spokesman Slobodan Vuksanovic told Reuters.

Parliament is due to meet in special session on Tuesday to consider a bill reinstating the opposition's gains in local elections in November. The socialistists annulled its victories on grounds of alleged irregularities.
Serbia has been shaken for three months by massive street demonstrations as well as sharp international criticism, both of which Milosevic appeared at first to studiously ignore.
He sent in his paramilitary police a week ago to forcibly break up protests in Belgrade. Scores of people were injured, provoking a new international outcry over police aggression.
But, apparently trying to repair what remains of his reputation abroad, he suddenly announced last Tuesday that he would ask parliament to reinstate the opposition's local election victories.
Milosevic told an Athens newspaper he was confident that parliament would do so. "I am optimistic that the bill will pass. It will be approved..." he said.
But the opposition says Milosevic can be expected to fight every inch of the way against its campaign to establish the independence of the media and judiciary.
"Difficult months lie before us," coalition co-leader Zoran Djindjic told Sunday's demonstrators in Belgrade.
"In our opinion, Milosevic...has no intention of raising the white flag, but only of consolidating his strength and then trying to win back what he lost personally."
He said Milosevic intended to reduce the already limited powers of local councils still further by stripping them of their sources of revenue.

The opposition wants to restore the independence of Studio B, a Belgrade television station taken over by the state. "He (Milosevic) can rest assured there will be hundreds of thousands in the streets again if he does not free it," Djindjic said.
Vuksanovic said he did not think the socialists would have any difficulty getting the bill through parliament on Tuesday although they alone do not have an absolute majority.
"The socialists have enough votes and can pass the draft (law) in five minutes just as they have done with all laws they have needed in the past," he said.
The opposition has started mapping out its strategy for presidential and parliamentary elections due to be held by the end of the year.

"There are oral agreements (among the Zajedno coalition's three partners)...The crucial question is to find the best means and the best people to realise our goals as quickly as possible and with the least possible risk," Vuksanovic said.
Vuk Draskovic, head of the Renewal Movement, told private BKTV television that Zajedno had agreed on the division of top posts if it were to take part in the next elections.
His party would nominate a presidential candidate, the Democratic Party the candidate for prime minister and the third partner, the Civic Alliance, a candidate for president of parliament.
